## Introduction

In this paper we construct and study a family of nonselfadjoint operator algebras that arise from unitary commutation relations between two collections of generating isometries. Specifically, we consider two finite sets of generators, $L_{e_1}, \ldots, L_{e_n}$ and $L_{f_1}, \ldots, L_{f_m}$, which do not commute in the usual sense but instead interact according to a *twisted* commutation rule of the form
$$
L_{e_i} L_{f_j} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{l=1}^{m} u_{i,j,k,l} \, L_{f_l} L_{e_k}, \qquad 1 \le i \le n,\ 1 \le j \le m.
$$
Rather than requiring the generators from the two families to commute outright, this relation allows one to "pass" an $e$-generator through an $f$-generator at the cost of redistributing the indices according to a fixed matrix of scalar coefficients. This construction produces a rich class of nonselfadjoint operator algebras whose internal combinatorial structure is dictated entirely by the coefficients $u_{i,j,k,l}$.

The key structural ingredient in this framework is the coefficient array $u = (u_{i,j,k,l})_{i,k=1,\ldots,n;\, j,l = 1,\ldots,m}$, which we require to form an $nm \times nm$ unitary matrix, when regarded as an operator on $\mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^m$. This unitarity condition is not merely a convenient normalization; it is precisely what is needed to ensure that the relations are consistent with the generators acting as isometries with orthogonal ranges, and it guarantees that the resulting representations behave well from an operator-theoretic standpoint. In this way, the matrix $u$ encodes all of the interaction data between the two families of generators: it dictates exactly how each pair $(e_i, f_j)$ factors when its order is reversed, and hence governs the full combinatorial and algebraic structure of the algebra it generates.

This construction should be viewed as a natural generalization of the analytic Toeplitz algebras associated to rank 2 graphs with a single vertex. In the rank 2 graph setting, one has two families of edges — again indexed by $1,\ldots,n$ and $1,\ldots,m$ — subject to a single-vertex factorization rule that identifies each product $e_i f_j$ with a unique product $f_l e_k$. Such factorization systems correspond exactly to permutation matrices $u$, i.e., unitary matrices whose entries lie in $\{0,1\}$. Our setup extends this picture by allowing $u$ to be an arbitrary unitary matrix, not merely a permutation matrix, thereby producing a substantially richer class of algebras that includes the higher-rank graph Toeplitz algebras as a special (combinatorial) case, while also incorporating continuous families of noncommutative "twists" between the generators.

The main achievement of the paper is a complete classification, up to isometric isomorphism, of the operator algebras arising from this construction. We show that two such algebras, built respectively from unitary matrices $u$ and $u'$ of compatible sizes, are isometrically isomorphic if and only if $u$ and $u'$ are related by an explicit and readily verifiable algebraic condition formulated directly in terms of the entries of the two matrices. This classification theorem reduces the (a priori difficult) isomorphism problem for these nonselfadjoint operator algebras to a concrete linear-algebraic question about the defining unitary matrices, thereby providing a complete and effective invariant for the isomorphism class of the algebra. In particular, this result recovers and extends known classification statements for rank 2 graph algebras with one vertex, situating them within the broader context of algebras generated by unitarily twisted families of isometries.

# Nonselfadjoint Operator Algebras from Unitary Commutation Relations: A Classification

## 1. Introduction

The study of nonselfadjoint operator algebras generated by families of isometries satisfying prescribed commutation relations has developed into a rich area connecting operator theory, graph algebras, and representation theory. A particularly fertile source of examples arises from higher-rank graphs (or $k$-graphs), introduced by Kumjian and Pask as a generalization of the Cuntz–Krieger framework to higher-rank combinatorial structures. When such a $k$-graph has a single vertex, the associated Toeplitz algebra is generated by finitely many families of isometries — one family for each "color" or rank — subject to relations that intertwine the generators according to a permutation of index sets. These single-vertex rank-2 graph algebras have proven to be a rich testing ground for questions about semicrossed products, free semigroup algebras, and noncommutative analytic Toeplitz algebras, since their generators can be organized into two commuting families of $n$ and $m$ isometries respectively, with the commutation between the two families encoded combinatorially by a permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}\times\{1,\dots,m\}$.

The present paper undertakes a natural and substantial generalization of this picture. Instead of restricting the interaction between the two families of isometries to be governed by a permutation matrix, we allow the intertwining relation to be specified by an arbitrary unitary matrix $u$ acting on $\mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^m$. This produces a much larger and more flexible class of operator algebras, which we call the algebras $\mathcal{A}(u)$, defined as the nonselfadjoint operator algebras generated by two families of row isometries $S_1,\dots,S_n$ and $T_1,\dots,T_m$ acting on a common Hilbert space, subject to the relation
$$
S_i T_j = \sum_{k,l} u_{(i,j),(k,l)}\, T_l S_k,
$$
where $u = (u_{(i,j),(k,l)})$ is an $nm \times nm$ unitary matrix. When $u$ is a permutation matrix corresponding to a bijection of $\{1,\dots,n\}\times\{1,\dots,m\}$, one recovers precisely the Toeplitz algebras of single-vertex rank-2 graphs studied in earlier work. The general unitary case interpolates continuously between these combinatorial models and allows for genuinely noncombinatorial, "quantum" commutation phenomena between the two families of generators.

## 2. Motivation and Context

Several strands of motivation converge in this construction. First, from the perspective of $k$-graph algebras, it is natural to ask what happens when the rigid combinatorial factorization rules of a higher-rank graph are relaxed to allow unitary (rather than merely permutation) intertwiners; this is analogous to the passage from classical Cuntz–Krieger algebras to twisted or quantum versions thereof. Second, from the perspective of noncommutative function theory, the algebras $\mathcal{A}(u)$ can be viewed as noncommutative analytic Toeplitz algebras associated to a "twisted free semigroup," generalizing Popescu's noncommutative disc algebras and the free semigroupoid algebras studied by Kribs, Power, and others. Third, unitary commutation relations of exactly this shape arise naturally in the study of Yang–Baxter type equations and in the representation theory of quantum groups, where families of creation operators satisfy braided or twisted commutation relations parameterized by an $R$-matrix.

Given this diversity of motivating contexts, a fundamental structural question presents itself: to what extent does the algebra $\mathcal{A}(u)$ remember the matrix $u$ that defines it, and conversely, when do two different unitary matrices $u$ and $v$ give rise to isometrically isomorphic operator algebras? Addressing this question is the central goal of the paper.

## 3. Construction of the Algebras $\mathcal{A}(u)$

We begin by constructing, for each $nm\times nm$ unitary matrix $u$, a canonical Fock-space representation of the relations above, built on the full Fock space over $\mathbb{C}^n \oplus \mathbb{C}^m$, twisted by the action of $u$ on the mixed tensor components. The universal algebra $\mathcal{A}(u)$ is then defined as the norm-closed nonselfadjoint operator algebra generated by the images of the canonical generators in this Fock representation. We establish that this representation is faithful in the appropriate sense, that the algebra $\mathcal{A}(u)$ possesses a natural expectation onto its diagonal, and that many of the standard tools available for single-vertex $k$-graph algebras — wandering vector arguments, Wold-type decompositions, and characterizations of the invariant subspace lattice — carry over to this more general unitary setting after suitable modification. We also examine the periodicity and gauge-invariance properties of $\mathcal{A}(u)$, and identify the appropriate notion of "rank-2 graph symmetry group" for a general unitary parameter $u$.

## 4. The Classification Theorem

The main theorem of the paper gives a complete answer to the isomorphism question posed above: two algebras $\mathcal{A}(u)$ and $\mathcal{A}(v)$, for unitary matrices $u,v \in M_{nm}(\mathbb{C})$, are isometrically isomorphic if and only if $u$ and $v$ are related by an explicit and checkable algebraic relation involving conjugation by matrices in $U(n) \otimes U(m)$ together with a possible relabeling automorphism arising from permutations of the index sets $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $\{1,\dots,m\}$. In particular, the isomorphism class of $\mathcal{A}(u)$ is completely determined by the orbit of $u$ under this natural group action, giving a clean and effectively computable invariant.

The proof proceeds by first identifying a collection of canonical invariants attached to $\mathcal{A}(u)$ — arising from the structure of its automorphism group, its lattice of invariant subspaces, and the multiplicity structure of certain distinguished representations — and showing that these invariants recover the orbit of $u$ exactly. Conversely, an explicit construction shows that any two unitary matrices in the same orbit yield isomorphic algebras via an isomorphism implemented by unitary conjugation of the generating isometries.

## 5. Consequences and Outlook

This classification provides a structural framework unifying and extending previous rigidity results for single-vertex rank-2 graph algebras, and it clarifies exactly which features of the combinatorial permutation data generalize to the fully unitary setting and which features are special to the combinatorial case. As applications, we recover known rigidity phenomena for $k$-graph Toeplitz algebras as special cases, and we identify new families of nonisomorphic algebras arising from continuous deformations of permutation matrices within $U(n)\otimes U(m)$, showing that the moduli space of isomorphism classes is genuinely richer than in the combinatorial setting. We conclude with a discussion of natural directions for further work, including the extension of this classification to higher rank $k \geq 3$, the study of the associated $C^*$-envelopes, and connections to quantum group representation theory suggested by the appearance of $R$-matrix–like unitary parameters in the defining relations.

# Toeplitz Matrices and Operators

Toeplitz matrices represent one of the most elegant and widely studied structures in linear algebra and functional analysis. Named after the German mathematician Otto Toeplitz (1881–1940), these matrices are characterized by a distinctive property: all elements along any diagonal running from upper-left to lower-right are identical. In other words, a Toeplitz matrix has constant values along each of its diagonals, meaning the entry at position (i, j) depends only on the difference i − j.

**Structure and Definition**

Formally, a Toeplitz matrix T is defined by a sequence of values {a_k} such that T_{i,j} = a_{i-j}. This creates a highly structured matrix where knowledge of just the first row and first column (or equivalently, the sequence of diagonal values) completely determines the entire matrix. For an n × n Toeplitz matrix, this means only 2n − 1 parameters are needed, rather than the n² parameters required for a general matrix.

**Applications**

These matrices arise naturally in numerous fields:

- **Signal Processing**: Toeplitz matrices appear in the study of linear time-invariant systems, convolution operations, and digital filtering.
- **Numerical Analysis**: They are fundamental in solving certain differential equations and in approximation theory.
- **Statistics**: Covariance matrices of stationary time series often exhibit Toeplitz structure.
- **Image Processing**: Two-dimensional generalizations (block Toeplitz matrices) are used in image deblurring and restoration algorithms.

**Toeplitz Operators**

Beyond finite matrices, the concept extends to infinite-dimensional settings through Toeplitz operators, which act on Hardy spaces of analytic functions. These operators are constructed by compressing multiplication operators to a subspace, and they play a crucial role in operator theory, particularly in understanding spectral properties and the theory of function spaces.

**Computational Advantages**

One of the most significant practical benefits of Toeplitz structure is computational efficiency. Due to their special form, many operations involving Toeplitz matrices—such as matrix-vector multiplication—can be performed in O(n log n) time using fast Fourier transform techniques, compared to O(n²) for general matrices. Additionally, solving Toeplitz systems of linear equations can often be done in O(n²) or even O(n log² n) time using specialized algorithms like the Levinson-Durbin recursion, rather than the O(n³) required for general linear systems.

**Conclusion**

The theory of Toeplitz matrices and operators bridges pure and applied mathematics, offering both deep theoretical insights into function theory and operator algebras, as well as practical computational tools used across engineering and the sciences. Their enduring relevance in modern applications—from telecommunications to machine learning—demonstrates the lasting significance of Toeplitz's original mathematical insights.

# Abstract

We study a class of nonselfadjoint operator algebras generated by families of isometries subject to unitary commutation relations, providing a unifying framework that generalizes the higher-rank graph algebras associated to single-vertex $k$-graphs. Given a unitary matrix (or more generally a unitary representation of a suitable coefficient system) encoding the commutation relations among generators, we construct a universal operator algebra $\mathcal{A}_\theta$ presented by isometries $s_1, \dots, s_n, t_1, \dots, t_m$ satisfying relations of the form $s_i t_j = \sum_{k,l} \theta_{ij}^{kl} t_k s_l$, and analyze its structure as a nonselfadjoint operator algebra. We show that these algebras admit a concrete representation as tensor algebras of an associated product system of Hilbert bimodules over $\mathbb{N}^2$ or $\mathbb{N}^k$, allowing us to identify their $C^*$-envelope explicitly and to describe the associated Cuntz-Pimsner and Toeplitz-Pimsner $C^*$-algebras. We establish criteria for these tensor algebras to be semicrossed products and determine when they arise from an underlying rank-$2$ (or higher-rank) graph, thereby recovering the classical graph algebra construction as a special case corresponding to permutation-type unitaries. We further investigate isomorphism problems for these algebras: we characterize when two unitaries $\theta$ and $\theta'$ yield (algebraically or completely isometrically) isomorphic nonselfadjoint algebras in terms of a natural equivalence relation on the defining unitaries, generalizing known rigidity results for higher-rank graph algebras. Applications include new examples of nonselfadjoint operator algebras with prescribed $C^*$-envelopes, a description of their Fock space representations and wandering vector states, and a classification, up to complete isometric isomorphism, within several natural subclasses defined by additional symmetry constraints on $\theta$.

# Classification of Operator Algebras from Unitary Commutation Relations

Here's a summary of this type of result:

## Setup

Consider operator algebras generated by two families of isometries (or operators) $L_e$ and $L_f$ satisfying a **unitary commutation relation** of the form:
$$L_e L_f = L_{\phi(f)} L_{\psi(e)}$$
or more generally
$$L_e^{(1)} L_f^{(2)} = \sum_{e', f'} U_{ef}^{e'f'} \, L_{f'}^{(2)} L_{e'}^{(1)}$$
where $U$ is a unitary matrix encoding how the two families "commute" past each other (generalizing the flip, or braiding-type relations).

These arise naturally from **product systems of Hilbert bimodules**, from **higher-rank graph algebras**, and from **Cuntz-Krieger type relations** twisted by a unitary.

## Main Classification Result

**Theorem (informal statement).** Let $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{U}'$ be unitary matrices (of the same size, indexing finite alphabets $E, F$) defining two such commutation relations. Let $\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{U}'}$ be the universal operator algebras generated by isometries satisfying these relations (the **noncommutative analytic Toeplitz algebras** associated to $\mathcal{U}$, $\mathcal{U}'$). Then:

$$\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{U} \cong \mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{U}'} \text{ isometrically isomorphic} \iff \mathcal{U}' = (V \otimes W) \, \mathcal{U} \, (V \otimes W)^*$$

for some unitaries $V, W$ acting on the coordinate spaces (i.e., $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{U}'$ are equivalent under **local unitary conjugation**), or more precisely up to the natural equivalence relation identifying unitaries that differ by "relabeling" the generators.

## Key Ideas in the Proof

1. **Fock space model**: Each algebra $\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{U}$ has a concrete representation on a Fock-space-like Hilbert space built from $E$ and $F$, with $L_e, L_f$ acting as (twisted) creation operators.

2. **Wandering vectors / vacuum vector**: The isomorphism is pinned down by tracking the image of the vacuum (or a generating wandering vector), since isometric isomorphisms of such algebras are typically implemented by unitaries that fix this vector up to scalar.

3. **Recovering $\mathcal{U}$ from the algebra**: One shows $\mathcal{U}$ can be recovered (up to the stated equivalence) from the algebraic/order structure of $\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{U}$ — often via examining the commutant, the invariant subspace lattice, or the "matrix of commutation coefficients" acting on the span of low-degree words.

4. **Completely isometric vs. isometric**: Often the classification is sharper at the level of *completely isometric* isomorphisms (rigid, forces $\mathcal{U}' $ unitarily equivalent to $\mathcal U$) versus merely *isometric* isomorphisms (where extra flexibility, e.g. via automorphisms of the underlying graph/alphabet, can enter).

## Context

This type of theorem appears in work related to:
- **Free semigroup algebras** and noncommutative Hardy algebras (Davidson–Pitts, Popescu)
- **Twisted tensor algebras** / **product systems** (Muhly–Solel, Kakariadis–Katsoulis)
- **Higher rank graph algebras and their Toeplitz algebras**

---

If you have a **specific paper or precise relation** in mind (e.g., a particular twisting unitary $U$, or a specific paper by Davidson, Kakariadis, Katsoulis, or similar), let me know and I can tailor the summary to match the exact statement, hypotheses, and invariants used in that result.

# Operator Algebras Generated by Isometries with Unitary Commutation Relations

## Definition

Let $u = (u_{ij})$ be a unitary $n \times n$ matrix (or more generally, a unitary operator on $\mathbb{C}^n \otimes \mathbb{C}^n$ satisfying suitable Yang-Baxter-type conditions). Consider isometries $S_1, \dots, S_n$ acting on a Hilbert space, subject to the **twisted commutation relations**:
$$
S_i S_j = \sum_{k,l} u_{ij}^{kl}\, S_k S_l, \qquad i,j = 1,\dots, n,
$$
together with the requirement that $\sum_i S_i S_i^* = I$ (so the isometries have orthogonal, jointly exhausting ranges — i.e., they form a **row isometry** or Cuntz-type family). The **operator algebra $\mathcal{A}_u$** is defined as the *norm-closed* (or WOT-closed, depending on context) algebra generated by $S_1, \dots, S_n$ acting on the Fock-space-like model built from the relations, i.e.
$$
\mathcal{A}_u = \overline{\text{Alg}}(S_1, \dots, S_n).
$$

The unitary $u$ encodes exactly *how* the generators fail to commute: setting $u = I$ (the flip, or identity) recovers various classical relations, while a generic unitary $u$ produces a genuinely noncommutative, braided family of isometries. This is a special case of algebras associated with **product systems** or **higher-rank graphs** with a single vertex and $n$ edges of two colors identified via $u$.

## How it Generalizes Analytic Toeplitz Algebras of Rank-2 Graphs

**Rank-2 graph algebras (Toeplitz algebras of 2-graphs).**
A rank-2 graph $\Lambda$ with one vertex and $m$ blue edges, $n$ red edges is governed by a factorization rule: a permutation-like bijection
$$
\theta: E_{\text{blue}} \times E_{\text{red}} \to E_{\text{red}} \times E_{\text{blue}}
$$
satisfying the **cube/associativity condition** (unique factorization of paths). The associated Toeplitz algebra $\mathcal{T}_\Lambda^+$ is generated by isometries $\{S_i\}$ (blue) and $\{T_j\}$ (red) satisfying
$$
S_i T_j = T_{j'} S_{i'} \quad \text{whenever } \theta(i,j) = (j',i').
$$
This is exactly the commutation relation above, but with $u$ a **permutation matrix** (a 0–1 unitary): the bijection $\theta$ is literally the special case of a unitary satisfying the Yang–Baxter equation with entries in $\{0,1\}$.

**The generalization.**
Replacing the permutation $\theta$ by an arbitrary unitary matrix $u$ (subject to the same Yang–Baxter/associativity-type condition ensuring consistency of relations, i.e. that the algebra is well-defined and the "cubic" relations close up correctly) yields:

1. **Continuous deformation**: Instead of a rigid combinatorial rule swapping two colors of edges, $u$ allows *coherent superpositions* — $S_iT_j$ becomes a linear combination $\sum u_{ij}^{kl} T_l S_k$ rather than a single swapped monomial. Rank-2 graph algebras are recovered exactly when $u$ is a permutation unitary.

2. **Same categorical structure, richer analytic data**: The associativity/Yang-Baxter condition on $u$ plays the role of the unique factorization property of the 2-graph, guaranteeing the algebra has a well-behaved Fock space representation, a "free semigroupoid"-type structure, and an analytic (creation-operator) model analogous to the analytic Toeplitz algebra $\mathcal{T}_\Lambda^+$ acting on $\ell^2(\Lambda)$.

3. **New invariants**: Whereas isomorphism/classification for rank-2 graph algebras is governed by combinatorial data (the permutation $\theta$, or its associated graph), for general unitary $u$ the classification requires *genuinely operator-algebraic and representation-theoretic* invariants (spectral data of $u$, its class up to natural equivalence, associated $C^*$-algebraic crossed products), reflecting the passage from a combinatorial/graph-theoretic world to a continuous, unitary-parametrized one.

In short: **$\mathcal{A}_u$ is what you get when you "quantize" the rigid swap rule of a rank-2 graph into a unitary scattering matrix**, keeping the isometric/Fock-space skeleton of the Toeplitz algebra construction but allowing the two families of generators to interact through arbitrary (Yang–Baxter compatible) unitary mixing rather than mere relabeling.

# Research Summary

## Nonselfadjoint Operator Algebras from Isometries with Unitary Commutation Relations

**Overview**

This research investigates a class of nonselfadjoint operator algebras generated by finite families of isometries $\{S_1, \dots, S_n\}$ acting on a common Hilbert space, subject to commutation relations governed by a unitary matrix $u \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ (or more generally $u \in U_n \otimes M_n$ in the multi-isometry block setting). The relations take the form
$$
S_i S_j = \sum_{k,l} u_{kl}^{ij} S_k S_l,
$$
generalizing the classical single-vertex rank-2 graph algebras, in which two commuting isometries satisfy $S_1 S_2 = S_2 S_1$ (the trivial permutation case $u = \text{flip}$).

**Motivation and Context**

Rank-2 graph algebras associated to a single vertex arise from a single unitary $u$ implementing a "flip" relation between two isometries, and their universal operator algebras—both C*-algebraic and nonselfadjoint (tensor-algebra) versions—have been studied extensively, revealing rich connections to noncommutative dynamics, Fock space representations, and Cuntz-type algebras. This work extends that framework to families of $n$ isometries governed by an *arbitrary* unitary matrix $u$, producing a much broader class of universal operator algebras $\mathcal{A}_u$ (and their C*-envelopes $\mathcal{O}_u$), realized concretely via generalized Fock space representations twisted by $u$.

**Main Results**

1. **Universal Construction:** For each unitary $u \in M_n(\mathbb{C})$ satisfying appropriate Yang–Baxter-type or unitary solution conditions, we construct the universal nonselfadjoint operator algebra $\mathcal{A}_u$ generated by isometries satisfying the $u$-twisted relations, realized faithfully on a Fock-space model.

2. **Classification via $u$:** We establish that the isomorphism class of $\mathcal{A}_u$ (algebraic, isometric, and completely bounded isomorphism) is governed by an explicit equivalence relation on the matrices $u$: two algebras $\mathcal{A}_u$ and $\mathcal{A}_{u'}$ are isomorphic if and only if $u$ and $u'$ are related by conjugation by a permutation-scalar unitary (or more generally by an explicit groupoid of "gauge" transformations arising from automorphisms of the generating isometries). This generalizes the known dichotomy in the rank-2 single-vertex case, where the flip solution gives a unique isomorphism class distinguished from non-permutation unitary solutions.

3. **C\*-envelope and Semicrossed Product Structure:** We identify the C*-envelope $\mathcal{O}_u$ of $\mathcal{A}_u$ and show it can be realized as a twisted semicrossed product or Cuntz–Pimsner-type algebra associated to a correspondence built from $u$, extending the identification of rank-2 graph C*-algebras as Cuntz-Pimsner algebras of correspondences over $\mathbb{C}^n$.

4. **Invariants:** We produce complete invariants for $\mathcal{A}_u$ up to the relevant equivalence (algebraic isomorphism, isometric isomorphism up to unitary conjugation, and stable isomorphism), expressed in terms of spectral and combinatorial data of $u$ (eigenvalue multiplicities, cycle structure when $u$ is a permutation matrix, and higher representation-theoretic data when $u$ is a general unitary solution to the braid-type relations).

5. **Representation Theory:** We classify the atomic and completely non-selfadjoint representations of $\mathcal{A}_u$, showing that the representation theory bifurcates according to whether $u$ satisfies the "cubic" or "permutation" condition, mirroring dichotomies known for two-generator rank-2 systems.

**Significance**

This work situates rank-2 single-vertex graph algebras within a unified matrix-theoretic framework, showing that the isomorphism problem for an entire family of higher-rank-graph-like nonselfadjoint operator algebras reduces to a tractable, purely matrix-theoretic classification problem for the parameter $u$. The results open pathways toward classifying tensor algebras of arbitrary higher-rank graphs with multiple vertices via analogous "block unitary" data, and toward new examples of noncommutative dynamical systems arising from quantum group and braid-group representations.

# Free Semigroupoid Algebras from Higher-Rank Graphs: Formal Setup

## 1. Preliminary Data

**Definition (k-graph).** Let $k \geq 1$. A *k-graph* is a countable small category $\Lambda$ equipped with a functor
$$d: \Lambda \to \mathbb{N}^k$$
(the *degree map*) satisfying the **factorization property**: for every morphism $\lambda \in \Lambda$ and every decomposition $d(\lambda) = m + n$ with $m, n \in \mathbb{N}^k$, there exist unique $\mu, \nu \in \Lambda$ with
$$\lambda = \mu\nu, \qquad d(\mu) = m, \quad d(\nu) = n.$$

We write $\Lambda^n := d^{-1}(n)$, identify objects with $\Lambda^0$ (vertices), and assume $\Lambda$ is **row-finite** with **no sources**: for every $v \in \Lambda^0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}^k$, $0 < |v\Lambda^n| < \infty$.

## 2. The Fock Space Representation

**Definition (Graph Fock space).** Let
$$\mathcal{F}_\Lambda := \ell^2(\Lambda)$$
with orthonormal basis $\{\xi_\lambda : \lambda \in \Lambda\}$. Define, for each vertex $v \in \Lambda^0$ and edge-type generator, the **left creation operators**
$$L_\lambda \xi_\mu = \begin{cases} \xi_{\lambda\mu} & \text{if } s(\lambda) = r(\mu) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
extended by linearity and continuity, where $r,s$ denote range and source maps.

These operators satisfy the **Cuntz–Krieger–Toeplitz relations**:
$$L_\lambda L_\mu = L_{\lambda\mu} \ \text{(when composable)}, \qquad L_v^* L_v = 1_{v\ell^2(v\Lambda)}, \qquad \sum_{e \in v\Lambda^{\varepsilon_i}} L_e L_e^* \leq L_v \quad (\text{projection at } v),$$
for each standard basis vector $\varepsilon_i \in \mathbb{N}^k$.

## 3. The Algebra in Question

**Definition (Free semigroupoid algebra).** The *free semigroupoid algebra* of $\Lambda$ is
$$\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda := \mathrm{WOT}\text{-}\overline{\mathrm{alg}}\{L_\lambda : \lambda \in \Lambda\} \subset B(\mathcal{F}_\Lambda),$$
the weak-operator-topology closed unital algebra generated by the creation operators.

The associated **norm-closed** object
$$\mathcal{T}_\Lambda^+ := \overline{\mathrm{alg}}\{L_\lambda : \lambda \in \Lambda\}^{\|\cdot\|}$$
is the *Toeplitz–Cuntz–Krieger algebra* (tensor algebra) of $\Lambda$; $\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda$ is its WOT-closure, generalizing the free semigroup algebras of Davidson–Pitts ($k=1$, single vertex case).

## 4. Structural Invariants

Key invariants used in classification:

- **The graph $\Lambda$ itself**, encoded via its 1-skeleton and factorization rules (equivalently, via the collection of commuting partial isometries and projections $\{L_e, L_v\}$).
- **Periodicity / aperiodicity**: $\Lambda$ satisfies the **aperiodicity (Condition (A))** if for every vertex $v$ there is $\lambda \in v\Lambda$ with $r(\lambda)=v$ such that no nontrivial "period" $p \in \mathbb{Z}^k$ makes the associated cycline subalgebra collapse — formally, $\Lambda$ has no local periodicity at $v$.
- **The wandering vector space / core reflexivity data**: the lattice of invariant subspaces $\mathrm{Lat}\,\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda$, and in particular the *reflexive closure* $\mathrm{Alg\,Lat}(\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda)$.
- **Wot-continuous characters / gauge automorphisms**: the canonical $\mathbb{T}^k$-action $\gamma_z (L_\lambda) = z^{d(\lambda)} L_\lambda$.

## 5. Classification Theorem (Schema)

The general form of the classification results (following Kribs–Power for $k=1,2$ and subsequent generalizations) is:

> **Theorem (Isomorphism/Classification).**
> Let $\Lambda_1, \Lambda_2$ be row-finite, source-free $k$-graphs.
> 1. **(Algebraic classification)** $\mathfrak{L}_{\Lambda_1}$ and $\mathfrak{L}_{\Lambda_2}$ are (isometrically) isomorphic as algebras if and only if there is a degree-preserving isomorphism of the underlying $k$-graphs $\Lambda_1 \cong \Lambda_2$, i.e. the graphs are identical up to relabeling.
> 2. **(Reflexivity)** If $\Lambda$ satisfies Condition (A) (no periodic cyclic components / aperiodic), then $\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda$ is **reflexive**:
> $$\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda = \mathrm{Alg\,Lat}(\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda).$$
> 3. **(Semisimplicity/Triangularity dichotomy)** $\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda \cap \mathfrak{L}_\Lambda^* = \mathbb{C}\cdot 1$ (i.e., $\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda$ is *maximal triangular*, analytic) if and only if $\Lambda$ has no cycles (is acyclic as a $k$-graph, equivalently the associated $C^*$-correspondence has no periodic paths).
> 4. **(Wot-closed ideal structure)** The WOT-closed two-sided ideals of $\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda$ correspond bijectively to *hereditary saturated subsets* (or more precisely graded ideal lattices) of $\Lambda$, mirroring the ideal structure of the associated Cuntz–Krieger $C^*$-algebra $\mathcal{O}_\Lambda$.

## 6. Typical Proof Strategy Ingredients

To phrase your own results, you will likely need:

- **Wandering vectors and the Fourier/gauge averaging** to recover $\Lambda$ from the algebra (recovering vertex projections as diagonal WOT limits, recovering edges via rank-one perturbations).
- **Beurling-type theorem**: classification of $\mathfrak{L}_\Lambda$-invariant subspaces via wandering vectors, generalizing Beurling's theorem for the shift.
- **Higher-rank Cuntz–Krieger uniqueness theorem** analogue at the algebra level, ensuring faithfulness of representations.
- **Kribs–Power / Davidson–Katsoulis–Pitts** techniques: use the $k$ commuting shift structures and the coordinate subgraphs $\Lambda^{\varepsilon_i}$ to induct on rank.
